title: Teach AI How to Code: Using Large Language Models as Teachable Agents for Programming Education
venue: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '24)
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can function as teachable agents in programming education, specifically for learning by teaching (LBT). The authors argue that conventional teachable agents are costly to build because they require manually authored domain knowledge and behavior models. They investigate how to make LLM-based agents act more like novice learners rather than overly capable assistants, and whether such agents can better support student knowledge-building during programming instruction.

The authors developed TeachYou, a web-based learning environment for introductory algorithm learning, and AlgoBo, an LLM-based tutee chatbot. Their approach includes a Reflect-Respond prompting pipeline to constrain the agent's knowledge state and simulate misconceptions, Mode-shifting to make the agent periodically ask "why" and "how" questions, and a Teaching Helper that provides real-time metacognitive feedback on learners' teaching strategies. The paper includes a formative study with 15 programming novices using a baseline chatbot, a technical evaluation of the prompting pipeline across algorithm topics, and a between-subjects user study comparing TeachYou with a baseline system lacking Mode-shifting and Teaching Helper.

The main empirical study involved 40 algorithm novices recruited on campus, mostly university students with limited prior knowledge of binary search. Participants learned binary search materials, solved a Parsons problem, and then taught AlgoBo in an online system. Participants were randomly assigned to either the full TeachYou condition or a baseline condition. The study took place in a programming education context focused on introductory algorithms, with all materials translated into Korean.

The paper concludes that the Reflect-Respond pipeline can make the LLM agent's knowledge more reconfigurable, persistent, and adaptable, enabling the simulation of novice-like misconceptions and learning progress. In the user study, TeachYou produced significantly denser knowledge-building conversations than the baseline (reported effect size 0.71), especially through agent-initiated elaboration questions. Teaching Helper supported reflection on teaching methods, although it did not produce significant gains in measured metacognition. Overall, the authors argue that LLM-based teachable agents can make learning-by-teaching more scalable, interactive, and pedagogically effective in programming education.

identified_tools.name: TeachYou
identified_tools.description: A web-based learning-by-teaching environment for introductory algorithm learning that integrates an LLM-based teachable agent and real-time metacognitive teaching feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the full intervention condition for binary search learning, combining AlgoBo's mode-shifting question prompts with the Teaching Helper to support learners teaching an AI tutee.

findings.finding_summary: In a between-subjects study with 40 algorithm novices, TeachYou improved the density of knowledge-building messages in learning-by-teaching conversations compared with a baseline system without Mode-shifting and Teaching Helper. The paper reports a significant difference of p=0.03 with effect size Cohen's d=0.71.
findings.measure: Density of knowledge-building messages in LBT conversations

findings.finding_summary: Teaching Helper helped participants reflect on their teaching methods and sequence their questions strategically during learning-by-teaching. However, the authors report that they could not observe a significant improvement in participants' metacognition.

identified_tools.name: AlgoBo
identified_tools.description: An LLM-based teachable agent for algorithm learning that uses a Reflect-Respond prompting pipeline to simulate prescribed knowledge states, misconceptions, and gradual learning, and uses mode-shifting to ask why/how questions.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the AI tutee that learners taught during programming education tasks; also technically evaluated for its ability to simulate constrained knowledge, persist knowledge state, and adapt to tutoring.

findings.finding_summary: In the user study with 40 algorithm novices, AlgoBo's questions led to more knowledge-dense conversations during learning by teaching. The paper reports p=0.03 and Cohen's d=0.71 for the improvement in knowledge-building message density.
findings.measure: Knowledge-building message density in LBT dialogues

findings.finding_summary: The technical evaluation found that the Reflect-Respond pipeline could effectively configure AlgoBo's problem-solving performance across algorithm topics and knowledge states. With an empty knowledge state, AlgoBo got all MCQs wrong; with factual and code knowledge added, performance rose, including perfect 3/3 scores on several binary search question types after correct tutoring.
findings.measure: MCQ performance under reconfigurability, persistence, and adaptability tests

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational LLM used here as the backbone model for the baseline teachable-agent chatbot and for system components in the proposed environment.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in the formative study as the backbone for AlgoBo-Basic, where 15 programming novices taught binary search to a chatbot role-playing a tutee.

findings.finding_summary: In the formative study with 15 Python novices, participants reported that teaching the chatbot helped them reorganize and recall knowledge, but dialogue analysis showed learning was limited mostly to knowledge-telling. Of 546 messages, there were 244 knowledge-telling messages but only 15 knowledge-building utterances.
findings.measure: Dialogue composition: knowledge-telling vs knowledge-building messages

findings.finding_summary: Participants were generally positive about teaching the chatbot and found the natural-language interaction intuitive and familiar, but many perceived it as overly competent and wanted more student-like questioning and mistakes. Two-thirds of participants commented on awkwardness caused by the chatbot's competence.
findings.measure: Participant perceptions of chatbot as learner and teaching experience

quality_tier_rationale: The paper includes a between-subjects user study (n=40) and a technical evaluation, but the evidence is primarily mixed-methods/HCI experimental rather than a clearly reported randomized controlled trial with full educational outcome validation. Reported outcomes focus mainly on dialogue quality and metacognitive process measures rather than standardized learning gains.
impact_tier_rationale: The main reported effect on knowledge-building conversation density is statistically significant with a medium-to-large effect size (Cohen's d=0.71), which meets the blue impact threshold.
